[Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#expectations-as-integrals) used independent draws from the passage-level Student-t posterior. Direct posterior draws are often unavailable. [**Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)**](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html) uses dependent states from a chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior target.

The [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd) defined the target as a conditional distribution after observing data, and the [Markov-chain page](markov-chains.qmd#the-markov-property) defined the transition dependence. Because chain states are not independent, covariance terms enter the variance of their average; the [variance--covariance decomposition](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) supplies that accounting.

We first connect dependent chain averages to posterior expectations, then run four chains for the passage-level model, and finally distinguish initialization, transition, and stationary distributions so that convergence language refers to the right object.

## Chain averages

For the passage-level Student-t model and a function $g$, the target is

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

Under conditions that make the chain ergodic,

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)})
$$

converges to $I$. Here *ergodic* means, roughly, that the chain can reach the target regions relevant to $g$ and eventually loses the influence of its starting state.

Four objects should remain separate: (i) the posterior target $\pi$, (ii) a transition kernel $K$ designed to preserve $\pi$, (iii) the distribution of $H_s$ at a finite iteration, and (iv) the empirical distribution of the realized states $\eta^{(1)},\ldots,\eta^{(S)}$. Stationarity means that starting from $\pi$ leaves the iteration distribution at $\pi$. Convergence means that an allowed nonstationary start approaches $\pi$ under additional conditions. Neither statement says that a particular finite run has explored every relevant region.

## Four dependent chains for the passage-level Student-t model

The code runs a fixed reproducible random-walk computation: four chains, 6,000 iterations, 1,000 warmup iterations omitted from summaries, and proposal covariance $(2.38^2/2)\widehat\Sigma$, where $\widehat\Sigma$ is computed from the normalized posterior grid.

The transition is fully specified here: propose from a symmetric normal random walk, compute the proposed-minus-current log target, and accept when `log(runif(1)) < min(0, log_ratio)`. The following [Metropolis--Hastings page](metropolis-hastings.qmd#proposal-and-acceptance) proves that this rule preserves the target. The factor $2.38^2/2$ is a common two-dimensional random-walk scaling heuristic, not a linguistic assumption or a universally optimal setting.

```{r}
#| label: run-provo-mcmc
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)
log_sum_exp <- function(x) { m <- max(x); m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) }
log_target <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]; sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(eta) -log_target(eta), method = "BFGS",
                  hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_target)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid_values <- as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")])
grid_mean <- colSums(grid_values * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(grid_values, 2, grid_mean, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))
proposal_cholesky <- chol((2.38^2 / 2) * grid_covariance)
posterior_cholesky <- t(chol(grid_covariance))
initial_z <- rbind(c(-2, -1), c(-.6, 1), c(.6, -1), c(2, 1))
initial <- t(vapply(seq_len(4), function(chain) {
  grid_mean + posterior_cholesky %*% initial_z[chain, ]
}, numeric(2)))

set.seed(2026101804)
iterations <- 6000L
warmup <- 1000L
chain_rows <- vector("list", 4L)
for (chain in seq_len(4L)) {
  current <- initial[chain, ]
  current_log_target <- log_target(current)
  mu <- sigma <- numeric(iterations)
  accepted <- logical(iterations)
  for (iteration in seq_len(iterations)) {
    proposal <- current + drop(rnorm(2) %*% proposal_cholesky)
    log_ratio <- log_target(proposal) - current_log_target
    accepted[iteration] <- log(runif(1)) < min(0, log_ratio)
    if (accepted[iteration]) {
      current <- proposal
      current_log_target <- log_target(current)
    }
    mu[iteration] <- current[1]
    sigma[iteration] <- exp(current[2])
  }
  chain_rows[[chain]] <- data.frame(chain, iteration = seq_len(iterations),
                                    mu, sigma, accepted)
}
chains <- do.call(rbind, chain_rows)
saved <- subset(chains, iteration > warmup)
diagnostics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(saved, saved$chain), function(x) {
  data.frame(chain = x$chain[1], mean_mu = mean(x$mu),
             mean_sigma = mean(x$sigma), acceptance = mean(x$accepted))
}))

quadrature_mu <- sum(grid$mu * grid$weight)
stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, max(abs(diagnostics$mean_mu - quadrature_mu)) < .003)
diagnostics
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-mcmc-dependence
#| fig-cap: "Successive post-warmup values of mu in chain one. Their local continuity makes the dependence visible."
chain_one <- subset(saved, chain == 1 & iteration <= warmup + 250L)
ggplot(chain_one, aes(iteration, mu)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey35", linewidth = .55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = quadrature_mu, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = .7) +
  labs(x = "Post-warmup iteration", y = "Passage-level contrast (mu)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The four acceptance rates and posterior means are computed from the actual chains for the passage-level Student-t model. Adjacent values are dependent, so 20,000 retained states do not generally contain the information of 20,000 independent draws. Later pages quantify that loss.

## Three distributions

The posterior target is defined by the likelihood and prior. The transition distribution moves from one state to the next while preserving that target. The empirical distribution of a finite run approximates the target and contains Monte Carlo error. Conflating these three objects makes it impossible to say whether a problem belongs to the model or the computation.

Omitting the first 1,000 states here follows the declared reference computation. In adaptive samplers, *warmup* also tunes the transition rule. No finite iteration marks a magical point of exact stationarity, and discarding states cannot repair a transition that misses part of the target.

## Recap and forward link

1. Target, transition, iteration, and empirical distributions are distinct.
2. Ergodic chain averages can estimate target expectations despite state dependence.
3. Warmup reduces sensitivity to starting values and may tune computation, but it cannot certify convergence.
4. More iterations reduce computation error without adding linguistic evidence.

The [Metropolis--Hastings page](metropolis-hastings.qmd#proposal-and-acceptance) derives the transition used here.

## Check your understanding

1. Why may a dependent chain average still estimate a posterior expectation?
2. What does warmup change in an adaptive sampler?
3. Why do more iterations reduce computational error but not posterior spread?
4. Which of the three distributions encodes the linguistic model?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. An ergodic theorem makes averages of dependent states converge to expectations under the chain's stationary posterior distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Warmup adapts computational settings such as step size and mass matrix; it also lets the run move away from its initial state before retention. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Iterations refine the numerical approximation to a fixed posterior; they add no linguistic observations and thus do not narrow that posterior target. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The posterior target, defined by the likelihood and prior, encodes the linguistic model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
